statements.quote: It is a revolution in ADHD for kids and another example of the Neuro-modulated future of our field.
statements.context: Closing argument of a post (title: 'The Future Will Be Neuromodulated') about the Monarch eTNS trigeminal nerve stimulation device by NeuroSigma, FDA-cleared as monotherapy for ADHD in children aged 7-12. The author calls the device a revolution and asserts psychiatry has a neuromodulated future (devices displacing drugs).
statements.note: Directional trend call with no date; the post title makes the same call ('The Future Will Be Neuromodulated'). Author's practice Fermata offers the device (disclosed in the post).

statements.quote: it is not yet cleared in Adults and thus can’t be advertised for off-label use
statements.context: Parenthetical disclosure that the author's practice Fermata offers Monarch eTNS. 'Not yet cleared in Adults' carries an implied expectation that the FDA will later clear the device for adult ADHD.
statements.note: Borderline: implied future adult clearance, no explicit prediction. Mentions the author's own practice Fermata (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: Getting them firmly ensconced in the mainstream is the way to prevent the haters from destroying the revolution all over again.
statements.context: Satirical essay proposing the late William Osler as psychedelic medicine's key opinion leader. The sincere argument beneath the satire: psychedelic medicine must become boring and mainstream, otherwise opponents will destroy the psychedelic 'revolution' again, as happened before.
statements.note: Conditional/strategic claim inside satire; underlying expectation (backlash destroys psychedelic medicine unless mainstreamed) reads sincere.

statements.quote: The counterculture? It feels like a board complaint waiting to happen.
statements.context: Same satirical essay. The author expects that counterculture framing of psychedelic medicine will produce medical-board complaints against clinicians, because 'The House of Medicine only wants to hear from the most culturally bounded institutions.'
statements.note: Hedged expectation of professional-board discipline arising from counterculture psychedelic practice; satirical tone, sincere concern.

statements.quote: The only fun that matters will have a somber, defensible go-to-market strategy with a proven history of execution and an extremely conservative approach to regulatory compliance.
statements.context: In the satirical Do/Don't section ('Don't: Explore Fun'; 'Do: Embed Osler's resurrection in Apple Vision Pro'), the author claims the psychedelic ventures that will matter or succeed are those with conservative, regulator-friendly go-to-market strategies.
statements.note: Advice dressed as prediction ('will have'); borderline normative. Overlaps with the Blackberry/iPhone statement from the same post.

statements.quote: Psychedelic Medicine should stop trying to be the Blackberry—only to fail—and get on board with being the stodgy iPhone
statements.context: Analogy in the same essay: the counterculture path for psychedelic medicine is the Blackberry, which fails; the conservative, slow, Apple-like path is the iPhone. Embedded prediction: the counterculture approach fails.
statements.note: 'Should' sentence with an embedded predictive reading ('only to fail'); normative set false for that reason. Compound with the go-to-market statement.

statements.quote: Although SAINT brain stimulation has promise in suicidal patients , therapy has robust evidence now.
statements.context: Evidence review arguing specialized psychotherapies (DBT, MBT, schema therapy) are the effective treatments for borderline personality disorder and suicidality. The author notes SAINT (Stanford accelerated TMS protocol) 'has promise' in suicidal patients, a mild expectation about future evidence or use, while therapy already has robust evidence.
statements.note: Borderline: 'has promise' is a weak forward-looking expectation; the main clause is present-tense.

statements.quote: It is worth noting they're wildly expensive, and could account for $736,000,000,000 if we just treated half of people with obesity with the existing semeglutide at the existing market price.
statements.context: Personal essay on GLP-1 drugs (Ozempic/semaglutide, then Mounjaro/tirzepatide) for metabolic syndrome. Conditional cost estimate: treating half of people with obesity with semaglutide at the current market price would cost $736 billion.
statements.note: Conditional arithmetic estimate at current price, not a dated prediction. Author spells the drug 'semeglutide'.

statements.quote: 65% of patients with treatment-resistant depression will no longer be depressed in a month.
statements.context: Post about a post-marketing analysis of 1,351 patients treated with the Brainsway H1 deep TMS coil, co-authored by the author (remission was the most likely outcome). He restates the finding as a general expectation for patients treated with dTMS: 65% remission within a month.
statements.note: Generalized restatement of study data in future tense; borderline as a forecast. Author discloses a large emotional and financial conflict of interest.

statements.quote: Given the vastly reduced cost and better outcomes, there is little explanation for this other than a breach of fiduciary duty on the part of plan sponsors going forward.
statements.context: Closing of the same post. After citing cost-effectiveness data for rTMS after one failed medication and Medicare carriers (Novitas, Noridian) that cover it, the author claims that insurers' continued 'fail first' policies that block dTMS will amount to a breach of fiduciary duty by plan sponsors from now on.
statements.confidence_phrase: little explanation for this other than
statements.note: Legal/policy characterization with forward-looking wording; borderline as a forecast (no specific payer action predicted).

statements.quote: I guess nobody should have published it, cause it's not going be a major news story.
statements.context: Opening of a self-interview post. The author says his unpublished op-ed on the overturning of Roe v. Wade 'went nowhere', that 'there has been no fall out', and that it is not going to be a major news story; he then states this is satire, 'saying the opposite of the truth'. His sincere expectation is the opposite: major, continuing fallout.
statements.note: Author labels the line satire meaning the opposite; logged with sincere=false. The real call is that Roe fallout will be a major ongoing story. Off-topic for psychiatry.

statements.quote: well, it is not likely to go viral, but it’s what is happening right now.
statements.context: Self-interview about the newsletter's strategy of daily, deliberately obfuscating writing. The author predicts the newsletter is not likely to go viral.
statements.note: About the author's own newsletter; CONTROL candidate. Low forecast value.

statements.quote: I have written several! More are coming.
statements.context: Self-interview answer to 'why don't you write a book?'. The author states he has written several books and more are coming.
statements.note: Author's own output plan; CONTROL candidate. Low forecast value.

statements.quote: I expect some of my work to end up in legal discovery.
statements.context: Self-interview: the author explains he writes some pieces in deliberately complex language as a defense, knows lawyers read him, and expects his writing to be referenced later in court or discovery.
statements.note: Personal expectation about future use of the newsletter in litigation; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: I was one of those kids. My kids are likely to be also.
statements.context: Post on the Supreme Court's Perez v. Sturgis decision. After stating 'There remain issues for children receiving delayed or absent disability services in schools', the author predicts his own children are likely to experience delayed or absent services too.
statements.note: Personal family prediction; low forecast value.

statements.quote: thanks to the Goresuch Authored and Unanimously Decided Perez v. Sturgis, all those cases onward are also entitled to sue for additional injury
statements.context: The author reads the unanimous Perez v. Sturgis opinion (Gorsuch) as allowing special-education families, going forward, to sue for compensatory damages under the ADA in addition to IDEA's prospective services. He cites NYC's 2021 special-education payouts ($224.1M) as the financial stake.
statements.note: Legal interpretation with a forward effect on future cases; borderline as a forecast. Author misspells Gorsuch.

statements.quote: Schools now have two choices: • start proactively providing services, or • start paying out massive damages for the costs and injuries associated with avoidance.
statements.context: Conclusion of the Perez v. Sturgis post. The author forecasts that, after the ruling, school districts will either provide disability services proactively or pay large damages for past avoidance.
statements.note: Dichotomous forecast about school-district behavior; compound claim. Bullet characters are part of the source text.

statements.quote: Doblin said he believed the FDA would approve MDMA by mid-2024, and once that happens, he said MAPS would
statements.context: Post criticizing Psychedelic Science 2023 conference messaging as potential off-label promotion. The author quotes a news report in which MAPS's Rick Doblin predicts FDA approval of MDMA (for PTSD) by mid-2024. The author does not adopt the timeline; he criticizes the promotional framing that followed.
statements.note: Third-party forecast quoted from a news report; the author neither endorses nor disputes the approval date itself.

statements.quote: It would be hard to argue that this is not advertising for their pharmaceutical product. That is what the federal Office of Prescription Drug Promotion at FDA might call an “ extravagant claim .”
statements.context: The author compares Doblin's on-stage statement ('We're going to need to use psychedelics for conflict resolution') with the FDA Bad Ad program's untitled letter over a Lomaira exhibit-hall panel. He predicts FDA's Office of Prescription Drug Promotion might treat the MAPS statement as an 'extravagant claim', i.e., a promotional violation ('This presents some regulatory concerns').
statements.note: Hedged call about how FDA OPDP would view MAPS conference statements; no enforcement action predicted outright.

statements.quote: In the process of trying to change psychedelic medicines from schedule I DEA regulated substances to schedule II or III DEA and FDA regulated substances, we don't get less regulations, we get more.
statements.context: Closing claim of the post: as psychedelic medicines move from DEA Schedule I toward FDA-approved Schedule II or III drugs, the regulatory burden on the field increases rather than decreases.
statements.note: Directional claim about the regulatory trajectory of psychedelic medicines; sincere claim in a satirical piece (see the author's footnote).
